$comment: Canonical viewpoints captured by `npm run shots` and diffed by `npm run shots:check`. Every entry is forced to hud=0&panel=0&freeze=1, because a visible HUD shows fps and heap and could never match between runs. Add a view per phase; never remove one without saying why in PROGRESS.md.

views.name: cube-default
views.expect: Default seed, three seconds of sim, camera near the ground. The baseline every phase is compared against.

views.name: cube-t0
views.expect: Sim tick zero, cube unrotated. Proves ?time= seeks rather than just pausing. Chunks are static, so the cube is the only thing that may differ from cube-default.

views.name: cube-seed-alpha
views.expect: Different seed: both the cube colour and every chunk colour change. Proves seed plumbing reaches content at every tier.

views.name: cube-wireframe
views.expect: Wireframe mode on from the URL, applied to the cube and to streamed chunk meshes.

views.name: cube-far
views.expect: Camera placed entirely from the URL, far from the default framing.

views.name: chunks-aerial
views.expect: Phase 1. Looking down on the streamed chunk grid from 300m. Every 64m cell is a flat colour derived from hash2i(coord, seed); a wrong colour or a missing cell is visible instantly.

views.name: chunks-aerial-seed-beta
views.expect: Phase 1. Same viewpoint, different seed. The grid layout is identical and every colour differs, which is what proves the seed reaches the chunk generator inside the worker.

views.name: chunks-radius-edge
views.expect: Phase 1, repurposed by Phase 2b. It used to frame the edge of the 512m streaming disc against the sky; with a 4km quadtree there is no such edge to see, so what it now tests is a mid-pitch view over several level boundaries at once. Its params are deliberately unchanged -- editing a canonical viewpoint destroys the only history the harness has.

views.name: chunks-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 1. Wireframe over streamed chunks. Guards renderer.invalidateMaterials(): meshes added at runtime are invisible to wireframe mode without it, and this view goes blank if that call is lost.

views.name: chunks-far-from-origin
views.expect: Phase 1. 200km from the origin, at chunk (3200, -2048). Proves the coordinate hash and chunk-local vertex positions survive large coordinates rather than degenerating into repeats or float mush.

views.name: terrain-mountain-profile
views.expect: Phase 2a. A mountain range in silhouette against the sky, 3.3km west of the origin on the default seed. This is the view that shows the height field is doing all four of its jobs at once: a continent shelf under it, a ridged multifractal peak, hillside relief, and slope/altitude colouring with a snow cap. If the terrain regresses to noise or to a plane, this view is the first to say so.

views.name: terrain-wireframe-relief
views.expect: Phase 2a. The same viewpoint in wireframe: the 32x32 (2m) triangle grid draped over real relief. Catches a change to SEGMENTS, a broken vertex grid, or a chunk that failed to build, none of which are obvious in the shaded view. Also re-tests the coordinate-derived renderOrder now that neighbouring chunks are no longer coplanar.

views.name: lod-horizon
views.expect: Phase 2b. THE SHALLOW-PITCH VIEW, and the reason it exists: every earlier canonical view is pitched down far enough that frustum culling throws most of the world away, so none of them can show what a 4 km quadtree actually costs or what its level boundaries look like. Here the camera is 5 degrees below the horizon with the snow-capped range 2-4 km out, so all five levels in play are on screen at once. Any crack at a level boundary shows as a sliver of clear colour through the ground; the skirts are what stop that. ~97 draw calls at 1080p against a budget of 1200.

views.name: lod-ground-horizon
views.expect: Phase 2b. The same terrain from 8 m above the ground, looking 1 degree below the horizon. This is where the lod-0/lod-1 boundary lands closest to the camera (about 320 m) and therefore where a crack would be widest in screen space. It also exercises the near-plane end of the depth range against 4 km of terrain, which is what the camera's near/far change was for.

views.name: lod-rings-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 2b. Straight down from 2.6 km, in wireframe: the quadtree's structure itself. The bright centre is lod 0, whose 2 m cells are sub-pixel at this scale and so read as solid fill; each step outward doubles the node size and halves the apparent line density. The stepped boundaries are the quadtree staircase. If the selection ever collapses to a single level, inverts, or stops tiling, this is the view that says so instantly -- and nothing else in the harness would.

views.name: water-coast
views.expect: Phase 3a. A coastline 900 m east of a headland on the default seed, with open sea beyond it. THE view that says the sea exists and is in the right place: sand at the waterline, turquoise shallows tracing the shore, deep navy offshore, and no hard line anywhere along the intersection. Every earlier canonical view was chosen before there was any water, and none of them frames a shoreline; without this one, a phase that stopped emitting water entirely would move a few pixels of colour and pass.

views.name: water-shoreline-shallow
views.expect: Phase 3a. THE SHALLOW-PITCH SHORELINE VIEW: standing on the beach 5.5 m above sea level, 3 degrees below the horizon, with the waterline a few metres away and the sea running to the horizon. This is the angle at which a hard intersection between the water plane and the ground is most visible -- a grazing view stretches a one-metre depth band across hundreds of pixels -- so it is where depth-derived alpha earns its place. If the alpha ramp is ever flattened, or given a non-zero floor, this view grows a crisp edge along the shore and says so.

views.name: water-bay-aerial
views.expect: Phase 3a. The whole bay from 800 m, where the depth shading is the subject: shallows follow the coastline as a turquoise band and the middle of the bay is nearly opaque navy. A flat, uniformly coloured sea passes `water-coast` and fails here. It also shows the water surface tracking a meandering coastline across many nodes at several levels at once -- if a node ever failed to emit water it would appear as a square hole in the sea.

views.name: water-bay-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 3a. The same bay in wireframe: the structural view of which nodes carry water at all. Water triangles are only emitted over ground below sea level, so the dense water grid stops at the coastline and inland nodes show terrain wireframe alone -- that is the discipline the whole phase's draw-call budget rests on, and it is invisible in every shaded view. Also catches a change to the water grid's resolution, which is deliberately the terrain's.

views.name: seed-canary-inland
views.expect: THE SEED CANARY, and it replaces `chunks-aerial-seed-beta` in that role. That view proved the seed reaches the chunk generator inside the worker by showing the same grid in entirely different colours -- but Phase 3a put sea level into the world, and on seed beta the origin turned out to be deep ocean, so it degraded into a nearly featureless blue field that a total seed-plumbing failure could shift by a few pixels and still pass. This position is dry on BOTH the default seed and beta, with real relief on each and height ranges that do not even overlap (default 15-120m, beta 107-232m), so terrain structure is the subject and the two seeds could never be confused. If the world seed ever stops reaching the generator, this image changes. Kept aerial at -72 degrees to mirror `chunks-aerial`'s framing.

views.name: river-valley
views.expect: Phase 3b. AN INLAND RIVER VALLEY on the default seed, at about 95 m elevation, 4.8 km north-east of the origin. The channel runs from the foreground into the middle distance with tributaries joining it, and the whole dendritic drainage network of the surrounding hills is visible as finer creases. This is the view that says flow accumulation is doing its job: a river network is not a wiggly line, it is a TREE, and a router that thresholded noise instead of drainage would produce disconnected scratches here. It is also the view that would go flat if `finalHeight` stopped carving -- the ground under it is ordinary hillside otherwise.

views.name: river-to-the-sea
views.expect: Phase 3b. THE VIEW OF THE PHASE: a full-strength river running from the foreground, through its own carved valley, into the sea. The acceptance criterion is that rivers reach the sea without terminating in mid-air, and this is where that is judged by eye -- the channel widens, its bed drops below SEA_LEVEL, and the Phase 3a water surface takes over with no join and no river-specific rendering at all. Sand banks appear along the lower reaches because the surface palette's shore band is anchored to the same SEA_LEVEL the carve drains to. A river that stopped at the coastline, or an estuary with a step in it, shows here first.

views.name: river-mouth-shallow
views.expect: Phase 3b. THE SHALLOW-PITCH RIVER VIEW: 60 m up, 6 degrees below the horizon, looking down the same river to its mouth. Every geometry budget in this project is decided near the horizon, because a steeply pitched camera measures frustum culling rather than the world -- so the phase needs at least one river view at that pitch. It is also the angle at which a carved bank reads as a bank rather than as shading: the valley wall on the left runs several hundred metres across the frame. If the carve profile ever grows a hard edge at the bank, this is where it appears.

views.name: river-mouth-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 3b. The same river mouth in wireframe: the structural view. Two things are only visible here. First, the carve lives in the ORDINARY terrain vertex grid -- there is no separate river mesh, no extra draw call, and the channel is a dent in the same 32x32 lattice every node has had since Phase 2a. Second, the water surface tracks the river exactly: water triangles are emitted only over ground below sea level, so the dense water grid follows the channel inland as a narrow ribbon and stops. If carving ever produced water where the ground is dry, or a channel the water failed to follow, this view says so and no shaded view would.

views.name: river-region-seam
views.expect: Phase 3b. THE REGION-BOUNDARY CANARY, and the single most likely visual failure of the phase. Straight down from 560 m onto the point where a strong river crosses x = 8192 -- a REGION boundary, 4 km of world -- so the boundary is the vertical centre line of the frame and the channel crosses it diagonally at the middle. Rivers are routed per region; a river routed only inside its own region stops dead at the edge, and at 4 km scale that reads as a wall across the world. Here the channel must run through the centre line with no change of width, depth or direction. Nothing else in the harness looks at a region boundary at all.

views.name: road-benched-hillside
views.expect: Phase 4a. THE SHALLOW-PITCH ROAD VIEW, and the one that says the phase happened. A road runs away from the camera up a shallow rise, its packed-earth surfacing following a bench cut into the slope, with the shoulder visible either side as a darker taper back into the grass. Every geometry budget in this project is judged near the horizon, because a steeply pitched camera measures frustum culling rather than the world, so the phase needs at least one road view at that pitch. Two failures show here first: a road that stopped being graded reads as a stripe painted over undisturbed relief, and a road that stopped being surfaced disappears into the grass while the bench remains.

views.name: road-wireframe-bench
views.expect: Phase 4a, AND THE VIEW THAT SAID IT WOULD SHOW PHASE 5. The same road in wireframe. The grading still lives in the ORDINARY terrain vertex grid -- the bench is a deformation of the same 32x32 lattice every node has had since Phase 2a, exactly as a river channel is, and the corridor is still only a handful of 2 m cells wide. What is new is the ladder of triangles lying along it: the Phase 5 deck IS its own geometry, in its own buffers, costing its own draw call, and it is the first thing since Phase 3a's water for which that is true. Its rungs are the deck stations, spaced at the node's own vertex spacing, and the pair of lines either side of the carriageway is the apron. This view is where a deck that stopped being clipped to its node, or started being emitted twice, would show as doubled geometry.

views.name: settlement-footprint
views.expect: Phase 4a. Straight down from 830 m onto a large settlement (radius 161 m) 2.6 km east of the origin, with a road leaving it to the south-west, a river system to the east and the sea in the corner. The footprint is a pad graded flat to the site's own altitude and surfaced as trampled ground -- deliberately weaker surfacing than a roadbed, because a village is cleared ground and a road is a made surface. This is where settlement SITING is judged: the pad must sit on gentle ground well above water, near fresh water but not in the channel. Since Phase 4b it carries streets; since Phase 6 the pad is filled with buildings whose roof plan is legible from this altitude as a warmer scatter inside the ring -- the before picture is gone, and that is the point of keeping the view.

views.name: road-river-ford
views.expect: Phase 4a, ANSWERED BY PHASE 5. THE COMPOSITION RULE, BY EYE: a road meeting a river channel 16 m deep. Rivers are applied first and the GROUND still yields to them completely -- grading moves no earth inside a channel, so there is no dam, and if that ever regressed the fill would raise the bed above the water surface and the river would visibly run over the top of it. What has changed is what happens above the ground: the Phase 5 deck is placed at the blended grading TARGET rather than at whatever the grading achieved, so where the ground stands down the deck does not, and the roadbed now carries across the channel instead of stopping at the near bank. The gap this view was captured to show honestly is gone, which is the whole content of Phase 5 in one frame.

views.name: road-region-seam
views.expect: Phase 4a. THE REGION-BOUNDARY CANARY, mirroring `river-region-seam`, and the most likely visual failure of any Region-tier phase. Straight down from 300 m onto the point where two roads meet at a junction and cross x = 4096 -- a REGION boundary, 4 km of world -- so the boundary is the vertical centre line of the frame. Roads are routed per region; unlike rivers they take NO cross-region blend at all, because each edge is routed in a window derived from the EDGE rather than the region, so one region answers each query and agreement is exact rather than approximate. The roads must cross the centre line with no kink, no step in width and no change in surfacing. A unit test asserts the same thing in bytes; this is the version a human can check.

views.name: settlement-streets
views.expect: Phase 4b. Straight down from 305 m onto the same settlement `settlement-footprint` frames from 830 m, close enough that the Sector-tier street plan is legible: an irregular ring at 0.58 of the footprint radius, spokes running in to the centre, and dead-end lanes running out to 0.78 of it. The road from the south-west crosses the ring and continues to the middle, and there is deliberately NO lane lying along it -- a candidate street within about 37 degrees of a road leaving the same settlement is dropped. Since Phase 6 the lanes are fronted by buildings, so the ring reads as a street plan with a village on it rather than as empty graded corridors; the view that says Phase 6 happened is `settlement-buildings`, one altitude lower.

views.name: settlement-streets-shallow
views.expect: Phase 4b. THE SHALLOW-PITCH STREET VIEW, standing inside the village about 15 m above its own graded altitude and looking east across it to the sea. Every geometry budget in this project is decided near the horizon, because a steeply pitched camera measures frustum culling rather than the world, so the phase needs at least one street view at that pitch. It is also the angle at which the grading is visible AS grading: the ring crosses the frame as flat, surfaced ground carrying the settlement's altitude out past the flat core of the pad, with the shoulder tapering back into the grass either side. If streets ever stop grading and become surfacing alone, this view goes flat while the aerial one barely changes.

views.name: settlement-streets-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 4b / 5 / 6. The structural view of a village. The street GRADING is still a deformation of the ordinary 32x32 lattice; on top of it sits the Phase 5 deck; and since Phase 6 the ring is lined with building outlines -- walls, gables and roof slopes as their own mesh, parented to the terrain node, in a third render-order band above every deck. Two failures show here first: a house whose winding is inside out shades black on one face, and a house emitted by two nodes doubles every edge along a chunk boundary.

views.name: settlement-sector-seam
views.expect: Phase 4b. THE SECTOR-BOUNDARY CANARY, mirroring `river-region-seam` and `road-region-seam` one tier down. Straight down onto x = 2560, a SECTOR boundary, so the boundary is the vertical centre line of the frame -- and this settlement's centre is only 74 m east of it, so its western lane and part of its ring lie in the sector NEXT DOOR, which owns no settlement at all. A sector lays out only the settlement whose centre it contains, so the ground west of the centre line is graded by a record belonging to the sector east of it; if a query ever read only its own sector, the village would be sliced off along this line. Nothing may change across it: no break in the ring, no step in the pad, no change in surfacing. Since Phase 5 the lane decks cross the same line without a seam; since Phase 6 buildings whose centres sit east of the line may overhang west of it -- ownership is by centre, not by clipping -- and that overhang must still be a single house, not a half or a double.

views.name: road-bridge
views.expect: Phase 5, AND THE VIEW THAT SAYS THE PHASE HAPPENED. A road crossing a tidal river on a bridge, 25 m above the water, with the deck spanning open water from bank to bank and the carriageway continuing on both sides. Everything about the phase is in this frame. The bridge is not a feature anybody wrote: the deck is placed at the blended grading TARGET and lifted to the ground wherever the ground is higher, so where `grading.ts` stands down completely -- which is exactly inside a carved channel -- the target is all that is left and the deck stays up. What must NOT be here is a causeway. The first attempt hung the apron to the ground unconditionally and produced a solid wall standing in the river from bank to bank, which is the dam `ROAD_RIVER_YIELD` exists to prevent, one layer up; `DECK_BEAM` is what stops the apron following the ground down, and if it is ever lost this view fills in solid.

views.name: road-bridge-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 5. The same bridge in wireframe, and the structural claim of the whole phase in one image: the deck is A SEPARATE MESH. The terrain lattice runs down into the estuary and stops at the shoreline, the water lattice covers the channel, and the deck crosses both as its own ladder of triangles belonging to neither -- rungs at the node's own vertex spacing, a rail either side which is the apron. Every phase since 2b added geometry to a mesh that already existed; this is the first that adds a mesh, which is why it is the first since 2b expected to move the draw-call budget. It is also where the clipping is legible: the deck is cut at each 64 m chunk boundary and each piece belongs to its own node, so a deck emitted twice, or a run that failed to stop at a boundary, shows here as doubled or missing rungs.

views.name: deck-lod-aerial
views.expect: Phase 5. Straight down from 1.6 km: two villages, the road joining them, the drainage network and the coast, all at once and all well past lod 0. THE REASON A DECK IS PER-CHUNK GEOMETRY. At this altitude every node on screen is at level 3 to 5, where the vertex lattice is 16-64 m and the Phase 4a surfacing -- which is a per-vertex colour on that lattice -- has washed out to a faint stain. The deck has not: it is exactly as wide as the road record says, because its width comes from the record and not from whatever lattice happens to be under it. That is the whole argument for building it per node against the node's own ground, and it is the difference between a road network you can read from the air and a smear. It is also the view where a deck that sank into a coarse hillside, or floated over a coarse valley, would be obvious. Since Phase 6 the two villages read as roof clusters rather than empty pads, which is the same claim one altitude higher than `settlement-buildings`.

views.name: settlement-buildings
views.expect: Phase 6, AND THE VIEW THAT SAYS THE PHASE HAPPENED. Straight down from 100 m onto the same settlement `settlement-streets` frames from 305 m, close enough that individual roof plans are legible: gabled boxes fronting the ring and the lanes, warm walls and darker roofs, a plinth of stone only where the ground falls away from the floor. Buildings sit on the street setback rather than on the carriageway, leave a gap between neighbours, and stop short of the pad's outer rim. Two failures show here first: a village of identical sheds means the tint and size salts collapsed onto one stream, and a house standing in the street means the clearance tests were lost.

views.name: settlement-buildings-shallow
views.expect: Phase 6. THE SHALLOW-PITCH BUILDING VIEW, standing just west of the ring about 9 m above the pad and looking east across the roofs toward the sea. Every geometry budget in this project is decided near the horizon, so the phase needs at least one building view at that pitch -- and it is the angle at which the FLOOR / PLINTH split is visible: floors hold a constant altitude while plinths meet this node's ground, so a house does not jump when the quadtree changes level under it. If floors were fitted per node the way a deck is, this view would shimmer as the camera moved.

views.name: settlement-buildings-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 6. The structural claim of the phase in one image: a building is A SEPARATE MESH, batched per node. The terrain lattice, the street deck and the house outlines are three distinct geometries; each house is 14 triangles (four walls, two gables, two roof slopes) with winding derived from an outward hint rather than assumed. Ownership is by centre and the geometry is not clipped, so a house whose centre sits in one 64 m node may overhang into the next -- and must appear exactly once. A plinth that hung unbounded down a bank would show here as a curtain of vertical edges.

views.name: vegetation-canopy
views.expect: Phase 7a, AND THE VIEW THAT SAYS THE PROP PIPELINE HAPPENED. Straight down from 180 m onto a forest patch west of the soak corridor (near the flight start at -6749,-4140). Trees and bushes are biome-scattered, owned by centre, batched into one submesh per node: a canopy reads as green blocks rather than as a draw-call bomb of one mesh per trunk. Clear of roads and empty of settlement clutter here -- the density claim of the phase, not the yard-prop half.

views.name: vegetation-shallow
views.expect: Phase 7a. THE SHALLOW-PITCH VEGETATION VIEW, standing just west of the same canopy and looking east through the trunks. Every geometry budget is decided near the horizon, so the phase needs at least one prop view at that pitch -- and it is the angle at which the BASE / STUMP split is visible: bases hold a constant sampleHeight altitude while stumps meet this node's ground, so a tree does not jump when the quadtree changes level under it.

views.name: vegetation-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 7a. The structural claim of the phase in one image: props are A SEPARATE MESH, batched per node. Terrain lattice and tree/bush boxes are distinct geometries; ownership is by centre and geometry is not clipped. A stump that hung unbounded down a bank would show here as a curtain of vertical edges, the same failure mode buildings have with an unbounded plinth.
